summary: Learn the common pricing models, what drives cost, and how to compare them for your restaurant.
intro:
A restaurant answering service cost usually falls into one of three buckets: per call, per minute, or a flat monthly fee. The real question is not just the sticker price, but what you pay when the phone is actually busy.

For a pizza shop, deli, or takeout counter, the cheapest option on paper is not always the cheapest on a full month. A better comparison is cost per completed order, plus how much time it saves your crew and how many calls it can handle when the line is ringing.

sections.h2: What does a restaurant answering service usually charge?
sections.body:
Most restaurant answering services use one of three pricing models.

- **Per minute**: common with human answering services.
- **Per call**: some services bill for each answered call or each handled call.
- **Monthly fee**: many AI phone tools charge a fixed monthly amount per location, often roughly **$79 to $599** whether or not orders come in.

Here is a simple way to think about it:

| Pricing model | What you pay for | Main risk for a busy restaurant |
|---|---|---|
| Per minute | Talk time | Long order calls get expensive |
| Per call | Each call handled | Short calls can still add up |
| Monthly fee | Access to the service | You pay even in slow weeks |
| Per completed order | Confirmed orders only | Less waste on non-order calls |

For owners, the key number is not the monthly sticker. It is the cost of one real order that reaches the kitchen. If you get lots of menu questions, reservation requests, or wrong-number calls, paying for every minute can feel expensive fast. If your phone is often busy at dinner, a flat monthly plan can feel simpler, but you still pay even when the phone is quiet. That is why many owners compare services by what a finished phone order actually costs, not by the headline price.

sections.h2: How do you compare per-minute, per-call, and monthly pricing?
sections.body:
Use one busy week as your test. Count the calls that mattered, then plug in your own numbers.

Say you take **120 calls** in a week and **40 become completed orders**. If a service charges by the minute, the bill depends on how long each order call runs. If it charges by the call, the bill depends on every handled order. If it charges a monthly fee, you pay the same amount whether those orders come in or not.

A simple comparison worksheet:

1. Write down how many calls came in.
2. Write down how many became orders.
3. Estimate average call time for each order.
4. Add any monthly base fee.
5. Divide the total by completed orders.

Example you can swap for your own:

- Say your average order call is **4 minutes**.
- Say you have **40 completed orders** in a month.
- A per-minute service can grow quickly if calls run long.
- A monthly plan might look easier, but you still pay during slow periods.

If you want a deeper pricing breakdown, see [per-minute vs per-order pricing](/blog/per-minute-vs-per-order-pricing) and [what counts as a completed order](/blog/what-counts-as-completed-order). The best choice is the one that matches how your phone really works: short questions, long orders, after-hours calls, and busy dinner rushes.

sections.h2: What hidden fees should I ask about before I sign?
sections.body:
Restaurant owners get burned by the extras, not just the headline price. Ask these questions before you agree to anything:

- Is there a setup fee?
- Is there a monthly minimum?
- Do I pay for test calls?
- Are after-hours calls priced differently?
- Do transfers, voicemail, or reservations cost extra?
- Is there a contract or cancellation fee?
- Do I pay even when no order is placed?

A practical phone script for sales calls:

> "Can you tell me the total monthly cost for one location, including setup, per-minute or per-call charges, and any other fees? I want to know what I would pay in a normal month and in a slow month."

For a small restaurant, the smallest line items can matter. A fee for each transferred call, a fee for each extra location, or a fee for simple questions can change the bill fast. That is why [hidden fees to look for in restaurant software](/blog/hidden-fees-restaurant-software) is worth reading before you buy anything tied to the phone.

Now add your own reality:

- If your orders are larger, the service cost may be a smaller share of the ticket.
- If many calls are just menu questions, a per-minute service can waste money on time that does not become revenue.
- If your phone is quiet on weekdays, a monthly fee may feel too high for the slow days.

sections.h2: What happens if the phone rings while you are busy or closed?
sections.body:
This is where phone cost and missed revenue meet. A service can look cheap until you realize it is only useful when it can actually catch the call.

For a lot of independent restaurants, forwarding matters more than fancy features. You can usually forward calls from your existing line to another number, and the method depends on your carrier or phone system. Codes vary, so always confirm with your carrier and test with a call.

Common examples:

- Many landlines and some carriers use **\*72** to forward all calls and **\*73** to turn it off.
- On some GSM mobile carriers, **\*\*21*number#** forwards all calls and **##21#** turns it off.
- **\*\*61*number#** can forward unanswered calls.
- **\*\*67*number#** can forward busy calls.
- Verizon Wireless often uses **\*72 / \*73**, and **\*71** for busy/no-answer forwarding.
- Business VoIP systems usually set forwarding in the web portal.

A useful checklist before dinner rush:

1. Forward the line you want to protect.
2. Test a live call from your cell phone.
3. Make sure the greeting sounds right.
4. Make sure the caller can order, ask hours, and get the address.
5. Turn forwarding off when you do not need it.

ROAL gives each location its own phone line automatically when you claim the host, and you can forward your existing number to it all the time, or only when busy or unanswered. You keep your own number, and forwarding can be turned off any time.

sections.h2: Is a restaurant answering service cheaper than phone staff or delivery apps?
sections.body:
It depends on what kind of work you need done.

Human phone staff usually bill per minute or per call, and you also deal with scheduling, training, and coverage gaps. Delivery apps commonly charge restaurants roughly **15-30% commission per order**, which can take a big bite out of a phone order if the customer would have ordered directly.

Try this side-by-side thought exercise:

- Say your average phone order is **$30**.
- If a delivery app takes roughly **15-30%**, that is about **$4.50 to $9.00** per order.
- If a phone service costs less than that and sends the order to your kitchen cleanly, the direct order can keep more margin in your restaurant.
- If a human answering service bills by the minute, one long call can cost more than a short order should.

This is why many owners compare [phone orders vs delivery apps](/compare/delivery-apps) and [phone staff cost](/tools/phone-staff-cost-calculator) before they decide. A phone answering service is not just about answering. It is about whether the phone becomes a clean order, a reservation request, a complaint, or a simple question that staff can handle later.

If your restaurant gets a lot of allergy questions, catering requests, or calls in another language, the right answer may be different from a simple message service. ROAL can hand those harder calls to staff with a summary, while still taking routine pickup and delivery orders from the live menu.

sections.h2: How do I choose the right plan for my restaurant?
sections.body:
Start with your busiest week, not your best sales week. The right choice should fit the way your phone actually works.

Use this quick checklist:

- Do most calls become real orders, or just questions?
- Do calls come in during rushes, after hours, or both?
- Do you need pickup, delivery, reservations, or all three?
- Do you want to keep your existing number?
- Do you need the kitchen to see the ticket immediately?

A simple owner test:

1. Estimate monthly completed orders by phone.
2. Estimate average order value.
3. Estimate what you currently lose when the line is busy.
4. Compare that with the service fee.
5. Decide whether you want predictable monthly pricing or pay-per-order pricing.

takeaways: Restaurant answering service cost is usually per minute, per call, or a monthly fee per location.
The cheapest-looking plan can cost more if your calls are long or your restaurant is busy.
Compare services by cost per completed order, not just the headline price.
Ask about setup fees, contracts, test calls, and extra charges before you sign.

faq.q: How much does a restaurant answering service cost per month?
faq.a: It depends on the pricing model. Many AI phone tools charge a fixed monthly fee per location, often roughly $79 to $599, while human services may bill by the minute or by the call. ROAL instead charges $0.90 per completed phone order, billed monthly, with no monthly fee or setup fee.

faq.q: Is per-minute pricing bad for restaurants?
faq.a: Not always, but it can get expensive if your order calls run long. A menu question, a modifier-heavy order, or a language handoff can add time fast. If your calls are usually short, per-minute pricing may be fine; if they are long and busy, compare it carefully against per-order pricing.

faq.q: What should I ask before I buy a restaurant answering service?
faq.a: Ask about setup fees, monthly minimums, cancellation terms, test call charges, and whether you pay for unanswered calls or simple questions. Also ask how the service handles pickup orders, delivery orders, reservations, allergy questions, and sold-out items. If you keep your existing number, confirm how forwarding works with your carrier.
